title: Speech at home
hookLine: your best self goes to the group chat; the lady Vedehika was gentle too, until someone pushed
tomorrow: a true thing, said at the wrong moment: is it still right speech?

lines: THE GROUP CHAT GETS THE BEST VERSION.
cards: The group chat gets the best version: patient, funny, generous with hearts. Then someone at home asks where the charger went, for the third time, and a voice comes out that nobody online has ever heard.

Same person, same afternoon, two completely different people. Why is kindness hardest with the people you live with? The Buddha told a story about exactly that, starring a woman everyone called gentle.

teach.h: THE LADY VEDEHIKA, KNOWN AS GENTLE.
teach.b: In the city of Savatthi lived the lady Vedehika, known all over the neighborhood as calm, gentle, peaceful. Her maid Kali, a good worker, wondered: is she really, or has nobody ever pushed her?

teach.h: KALI GETS UP LATE, THREE TIMES.
teach.b: So one morning Kali got up late. Hey, Kali! Yes, madam?
Why so late? Oh, no reason. Vedehika frowned.
The next day Kali slept later, and Vedehika snapped. On the third day, later still, Vedehika lost her temper and struck her with the pin from the door.
Kali ran out to the neighbors, and by evening the gentle lady's name had flipped. The Buddha's point is uncomfortable: a person is only as gentle as the first time disagreeable words touch them.
Then he names five ways anyone may speak to us: at the right time or not, true or not, gentle or harsh, helpful or not, with goodwill or with hate. Any of the five can come.
The training is to keep the mind unchanged, let no harsh words out, and stay with goodwill toward the one speaking.

Home is where all five arrive, early and late, from people who know exactly where it hurts. There's no audience to perform for, no reputation to protect, and nobody leaves when the conversation goes badly.
That's why it's hardest there. And it's also why a family can tell, better than any neighbor, whether the gentleness is real. The Buddha doesn't ask anyone to pretend nothing stings.
He asks that the sting not get the last word.

how: Right speech is one step of the eightfold path; Buddhist teachers often point lay students to MN 21's five ways of speaking when they talk about patience with family.

o: a rule of silence kept inside a monastery
speaking only your family's home language
right speech with family, where it's tested most

games.q: Vedehika's three mornings — tap the pairs.
p: known all over town as gentle
got up late to test her
Vedehika struck her with the door pin
mind unchanged, no harsh words, goodwill

s: in the story, Vedehika was gentle all along, and Kali lied about her
she frowned, then snapped, then struck. her calm held only while nobody pushed.
the Buddha names five ways anyone may speak to us, including harsh and untrue
at the right time or not, true or not, gentle or harsh, helpful or not, with goodwill or hate.
right speech means only speaking kindly to people who are kind to you
the training is to keep goodwill whichever of the five ways someone speaks.

games.q: your sister snaps at you before school for using all the hot water. you're tired and she's not wrong. what does the Buddha's training ask you to keep?
o: an honest, sharp reply, because true speech matters more than gentle speech.
a mind unchanged, no harsh words back, and goodwill toward her.
a calm face on the outside, while you hold the grudge for later.
games.why: MN 21's training is to keep the mind unchanged, let no harsh words out, and stay with goodwill, whichever way someone speaks.

practice: Say one plain, kind sentence out loud, softly, the kind you could say at home today: thanks for dinner, or, I'm glad you're here. Say it twice, slowly. Then sit with how it feels in your mouth, and who it was for.
If nothing comes, the plainest sentence works too: good night, sleep well.

wordCard.voice: Speech at home: right speech where it's tested, with people who can push every button. Gentle counts most when pushed.

orig.note: Pali: right speech, one step of the eightfold path.

carryVoice: Your line: kind at home, the place it's hardest. One of four, on speech at home.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 21 (Kakacupama Sutta: the lady Vedehika of Savatthi and her maid Kali; the five ways others may speak; the training to keep the mind unaffected, utter no evil words, and abide with goodwill)
